sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E2632. Attribution follows conversational context rather than ideological content or anchors alone. The transcript contains transcription errors and several events spanning speaker changes; these are marked U where inseparable. No audio verification was available. No edited teaser replays were identifiable.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: it's only those who say that they know they are certain who we have to distrust a priori
candidates.explanation: The maxim makes professed certainty grounds for advance distrust and exclusion from argument (E437–449). Human ignorance supplies a caution, but not the missing reason that revelation cannot convey knowledge. Hitchens grants a creator hypothetically (E383–408); that concession does not justify dismissing every claimed knower before examining their evidence.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: even though emotionally its proponents seem unable to take this on board
candidates.explanation: Lennox gives an evolutionary reliability argument (E774–786), so its disputed inference is not automatically slogan substitution. The additional diagnosis at E790–792 nevertheless explains proponents' nonacceptance through emotional incapacity rather than their objections. This protects that conclusion locally, although the qualified word 'seem' limits the strength of the diagnosis.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: to this day we have no other option
candidates.explanation: Lennox approvingly quotes the claim that Christianity alone grounds Western freedoms, dismissing alternatives as 'postmodern chatter' (E830–837). His university and legal-history assertions (E837–843) offer historical support, but do not establish exclusive present necessity. The categorical affirmation supplies that missing step; the dismissive phrase does not itself establish systematic protection against criticism.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: his plans are much bigger than we see
candidates.explanation: A future creation answers Hitchens's destruction objection by placing this universe inside a larger divine plan (E1290–1308). That could shelter design from adverse outcomes, but Lennox invokes a specific scriptural expectation rather than expressly accommodating every possible outcome. His later evidence condition (E1349–1357) further prevents confidently classifying this as unrestricted protection.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: neither of these propositions is worthy of the consideration of an intelligent or educated human being
candidates.explanation: Hitchens supplies objections concerning prophecy construction and conflicting religious authorities (E1642–1705), so the dismissal partly summarizes an argument. But E1706–1710 also makes consideration itself incompatible with intelligence or education, discouraging merits-based reopening. Whether the catchphrase replaces additional reasoning or merely intensifies the preceding conclusion remains uncertain.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: it shows that it doesn't lie in the chromosomes
candidates.explanation: Lennox presents genetic similarity as compatible with, and clarifying, human distinctiveness (E2047–2054). This might move the claim beyond contrary evidence, but he previously acknowledged that humans are animals (E1987–1991), and requests an open discussion rather than excluding all biological findings. The text cannot establish an unrestricted protective reinterpretation.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: I can only speak for my myself
contrasts.explanation: Hitchens explicitly limits his account of transcendence to personal experience, distinguishes subjective experience from objective applicability, and offers concrete experiential sources. This is a qualified interpretation rather than a catchphrase offered as public proof.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: Freud cannot help you at all on the question of whether God exists or not
contrasts.explanation: Lennox explains how comfort-based psychological accounts could run in either direction, then distinguishes those accounts from establishing whether God exists. The conclusion follows the stated symmetrical reasoning rather than substituting an accusation of wish fulfillment for evidence.
